sam.name: Sam Park
sam.role: engineer (someone who designs and builds things to solve problems)

case.title: The Speed Limit Sign
case.hook: After the fender bender, the pier manager wants a speed limit for golf carts. Gus says speed doesn’t matter, and he says he already tested it. Gus, Rosa and I each sealed a prediction in an envelope. Before anyone opens them, we test.

notice.head: PALMETTO BEACH PIER · NOTICE
notice.title: Coming soon: a cart speed limit
rows: Last Tuesday, a golf cart bumped Rosa’s ice cream cart.
If a cart bumps something, the thing it hits must not roll more than 2 feet.
notice.line: Three sealed predictions are pinned below.

memo.t: I already tested it! I rolled a BIG marble down the low ramp, and a SMALL marble down the high ramp. Both pushed the block about the same. One try each. So speed doesn’t matter. Any speed limit is fine!

envelopes.inside: Speed doesn’t matter. A bump is a bump.
envelopes.verdict: ✗ Not supported. His test changed two things and ran only one try.

envelopes.inside: A faster cart will push my cart farther. At 5 mph it rolled 3 feet!
Faster means farther. I’ll trust it after many fair trials.

case.envLine: No peeking! They open when you crack the case.
case.envOpen: The envelopes are open! Whose prediction did the trials support?
case.question: Gus says speed doesn’t matter in a bump. Rosa and Sam say a faster cart pushes farther. Whose prediction do the trials support, and how do you know?
case.how: Find 4 clues as you work through the lesson. Then crack the case (solve it) at the top of the Assignment tab.

clues.t: Your ghost marbles were predictions placed BEFORE the roll. Comparing them to where the real marbles stopped showed what you got right and what surprised you.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 1: the I-knew-it trap
clues.t: Only notes written BEFORE the test can be checked. A wrong prediction is still useful: it shows what you didn’t know yet.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 2: the flag lane
clues.t: Change ONE thing (the ramp height) and run several trials: the high ramp pushed the block farther every time, except one bumpy trial. One try alone can fool you.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 3: the Newton’s cradle
clues.t: Pull back 1, 2 or 3 balls: the same number flew out, trial after trial. When a pattern repeats, you can trust it and use it to predict.

solve.title: Whose prediction do the trials support?
solve.q: Which answer fits all four clues?

options.t: Gus’s. His test proved that speed doesn’t matter.
options.why: Check Clue 3. How many things did Gus change at once? How many tries did he run?

options.t: Rosa’s and Sam’s. In fair trials that changed only the ramp, the faster marble pushed the block farther, again and again.
options.why: Case cracked! Many fair trials showed the same pattern: faster pushes farther. The envelopes are open, and the sign is ready to make just below.

options.t: Nobody’s. Predictions can be wrong, so we can’t know.
options.why: Check Clue 2. A wrong prediction still teaches you something, and trials give you evidence.

options.t: Just do one more bump. One try will settle it.
options.why: Check Clue 3. Remember the bumpy trial? One try alone can fool you.

ghosts.title: Ghost marbles

hook.alt: A real Newton’s cradle: five shiny steel balls hang from thin strings on a metal frame. The two end balls are swinging out.
hook.cap: A real Newton’s cradle. Pull back two balls and let go. How many fly out the other side?
hook.credit: “Newton's Cradle” by Sheila Sund from Salem, United States, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

todo: Drag each see-through ghost marble down onto the board, where you think that marble will stop. (Or tap a ghost, then tap the board.)
Press Play. The real marbles roll, and your ghosts stay put.
How close were you? Do both rounds.

why.t: A ghost marble is your prediction. You place it BEFORE the test, so afterward you can check it.

ghosts.trayWord: Ghost marbles: drag each one down onto the board

rounds.sub: the BIG marble rolls into the small one.
rounds.alt: A model: a big blue marble rolls along a board toward a small orange marble that is sitting still.
rounds.line: The big marble kept rolling, slower. The small marble shot far away.

rounds.sub: the SMALL marble rolls into the big one.
rounds.alt: A model: a small orange marble rolls along a board toward a big blue marble that is sitting still.
rounds.line: Surprise for many people: the small marble BOUNCED BACK, and the big one only rolled a little.

ghosts.placeMiss: Drag both ghost marbles down onto the board first. They are your prediction!
ghosts.gapWord: How far off my ghosts were
ghosts.q: Why did you place the ghosts BEFORE pressing Play?

opts.t: So I could check my prediction against what really happened.
So the marbles would roll where my ghosts were.
opts.miss: Did the real marbles follow your ghosts, or did they go their own way?

opts.t: It doesn’t matter. I could place them after.
opts.miss: If you place them after you watch, is that still a prediction?

ghosts.win: Ghosts first, then the test. That’s how you check a prediction. Clue 1!

iknewit.title: The “I knew it!” trap
todo: Sam tested a small marble rolling into a big one at 8:15 PM. Read each pier kid’s sticky note and its time.
Drag each note to BEFORE or AFTER the test (or tap a note, then a side).
Then the result comes in. Stamp the wrong prediction.

why.q: What’s a sticky note doing here?
why.t: Pier kids watched Sam’s test and wrote notes. The time on each note shows when they wrote it.

iknewit.timeMiss: Look at the time on the note. The test was at 8:15 PM.

notes.t: I predict the small marble will bounce back, because the big one is heavier.
notes.miss: Mia wrote at 8:02. Is that before or after 8:15?

notes.t: I KNEW the small one would bounce back!
notes.miss: Leo wrote at 8:16, one minute after the test.

notes.t: I predict the small marble will push the big one far away.
notes.miss: Ava wrote at 8:05. The test was at 8:15.

notes.t: Obviously the big one would barely move. I could have told you.
notes.miss: Jay wrote at 8:20. The test was over by then.

q1.q: Leo says he knew it. Why doesn’t his note count as a prediction?

opts.t: He wrote it AFTER the test, so nobody can check it.

opts.miss: Mia was right too, and her note counts. Look at the times.
Mia’s and Ava’s sticky notes count. What’s different about Leo’s?

result.head: The result: the small marble bounced back, and the big one rolled a little.
result.t: Mia’s prediction was right. Ava’s was wrong.

wrong.q: Ava’s prediction was wrong. Stamp it:

stamps.miss: Did Ava learn something from her wrong prediction? A wrong prediction is not a failed test.

iknewit.q: What did Ava’s wrong prediction teach her?

opts.t: A small marble can’t push a heavy one far. It bounces back instead.
That she should stop making predictions.
opts.miss: Then she’d never learn anything new! What did the test show her?
Wrong predictions often teach the most. What surprised her?

iknewit.win: Write it BEFORE, check it AFTER, and learn from the wrong ones. Clue 2!

flaglane.title: The flag lane
todo: Drag the yellow flag to where you think the red block will stop (or tap the board).
Press Roll the marble. The yellow tape shows your gap.
Do 3 trials on the low ramp, then 3 on the high ramp. Watch your gap meter.

why.t: Your flag is your prediction. The gap between the flag and the block shows how close you were.

flaglane.alt: A model: a ramp on the left, a marble at the top, a red wooden block at the bottom, and a ruler in centimeters along the board.
flaglane.keep: Kept the same: the marble, the block and the board.

trials.note: Now you know about where a low-ramp marble pushes the block.
Close to the first trial, but not exactly the same.
Three trials, all close together: a pattern!
The higher ramp made a faster marble, and the block went much farther.
Way off! The block caught on a gap between the boards. If this were your ONLY trial, you’d think the high ramp didn’t matter.
Back to the pattern. Trial 5 was a fluke (a weird one-time result).

flaglane.flagWord: Drag the flag to where you think the block will stop
flaglane.flagMiss: Plant your flag first: drag it to where you think the block will stop.
flaglane.switchLine: Now change ONE thing: the ramp height. The marble, the block and the board stay the same.
flaglane.meterLabel: Gap meter: how far off was each flag?
flaglane.closerLine: Your flag got closer as you learned the pattern!
flaglane.useLine: Use the pattern in your table to place the next flag.

gus.t: I rolled a BIG marble down the low ramp, and a SMALL marble down the high ramp. Both pushed the block about the same. One try each. So speed doesn’t matter!
gus.q: Tap the 2 problems with Gus’s test.

opts.t: He changed two things at once: the ramp AND the marble.
opts.yes: Two changes at once: we can’t tell which one made the difference.

opts.t: He wrote down a prediction first.
opts.miss: Writing a prediction first is a GOOD thing. Look for something he did wrong.

opts.t: He ran only one try of each.
opts.yes: One try can be a fluke, like our bumpy trial 5.

opts.miss: We used a block too. That part is fine.

flaglane.win: One thing changed, many trials, and a clear pattern: faster pushes farther. Clue 3!

cradle.title: Pull, predict, let go
todo: Pick how many balls to pull back: 1, 2 or 3.
Predict how many will fly out the other side.
Drag the end ball back and let go (or press Let go). Run 3 trials of each.

why.t: A row of same-size steel balls hanging from strings. It’s named after Isaac Newton, a scientist who studied how things move.

cradle.alt: A model of a Newton’s cradle: five steel balls hanging in a row from strings on a frame.
cradle.pullQ: 1. How many balls will you pull back?
cradle.predQ: 2. Predict: how many balls will fly out the other side?
cradle.dragLine: 3. Drag the end ball back and let go, or press Let go.
cradle.pullMiss: First pick how many balls to pull back.
cradle.predMiss: Predict first: how many will fly out?
cradle.doneMiss: You did all 3 trials for this one. Pick another number.
cradle.wrongPre: Surprise! A wrong prediction still teaches you something.
cradle.againLine: Run it again. Does the same thing happen?
cradle.doneLine: Same every time: that’s a pattern. Try another number.

photo.head: The real thing
photo.alt: A real Newton’s cradle: five shiny steel balls on strings. The two end balls are swinging out, one on each side, and the middle three hang still.
photo.cap: A real Newton’s cradle. Here someone let go of BOTH end balls at once, so one ball bounces out on each side and the middle three stay still. The balls are all the same size, so each click passes the motion along the row.
photo.credit: “Newton's Cradle” by Sheila Sund from Salem, United States, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

cradle.slowLine: Why does it slowly stop? Every CLICK turns a little of the energy into sound and heat (and the balls push through air). So each swing is a little smaller.
cradle.q: You pulled back 1, 2 and 3 balls, 3 trials each. What pattern did you find?

opts.t: The same number of balls flew out as I pulled back, every time.
Always just one ball flew out.
opts.miss: Look at your table. What happened when you pulled back 3?
Look across each row of your table. Did the trials match?

cradle.win: Pull 1, 1 flies out. Pull 2, 2 fly out. Every trial! A pattern you can predict with. Clue 4!

cradlefree.sizeWord: How many balls on the cradle?

signmaker.title: Make the speed limit sign
todo: Read Ms. Okafor’s rule and Sam’s test results.
Pick the speed limit the pattern supports.
Tell how you knew, then stamp the sign.

why.q: Nobody tested every speed. Can you still choose?
why.t: Yes! A pattern from your trials lets you predict speeds you didn’t test. That’s what patterns are for.

signmaker.lockLine: Crack the case first. Then make the sign.
signmaker.rule: Ms. Okafor’s rule: if a cart bumps something, the thing it hits must not roll more than 2 feet.

data.head: Sam’s night test: a cart bumps a parked cart (3 trials each, averaged)
data.note: And Gus’s real bump: at 5 mph, Rosa’s cart rolled about 3 feet.

signmaker.pickQ: Which speed limit keeps a bumped cart under 2 feet?

opts.line: 3 mph is between 2 and 4 mph on the table, so a bumped cart would roll about 1 foot. Under 2 feet!
Gus’s real bump was at 5 mph, and Rosa’s cart rolled about 3 feet. Too far!
Faster than anything Sam tested. The pattern says much more than 4½ feet. Way too far!
The pattern says faster pushes MUCH farther. Way too far!

signmaker.q: Nobody tested 3 mph. How did you know it would work?

qopts.t: The pattern: faster pushes farther, so 3 mph lands between 2 and 4 mph.

qopts.miss: It was more than a guess! What did the table show as the speed went up?
Gus said speed doesn’t matter. What did the trials say?

signmaker.sign: Approved by Ms. Okafor, pier manager
signmaker.win: APPROVED! The pier’s new sign says 3 mph, about walking speed. Your trials and your pattern made a real rule.

q1.A: Think about the ghost marbles: your ghost and the real marble were in different places.
q1.B: Predictions can be wrong, like Ava’s. Which one comes BEFORE the test?

q2.B: Remember the flag lane? What did the extra trials show that one trial couldn’t?
q2.C: Your first flag lane trial wasn’t wrong. Why run more?

q3.A: Ava didn’t ignore her result. What did she learn?
q3.C: A test with a surprise result is still a good test. What should you do with new evidence?

welcome.label: Welcome · the speed limit sign
welcome.script: Hi, it’s Sam! The pier manager wants a speed limit for golf carts. Read her notice. Gus says speed doesn’t matter, and he tested it once. Read his note. Gus, Rosa and I each sealed a prediction in an envelope. We open them when the case is cracked.

warmup.label: Warm-Up · ghost marbles (Clue 1)
warmup.script: Look at the photo of the Newton’s cradle. If you pull back two balls, how many fly out? Write your prediction in the box. Then drag each ghost marble down to where you think the real marble will stop, and press Play.

vocab.notes: Hold up a sticky note for “prediction”; roll a ball twice for “trial”.

part1.label: Part 1 · the I-knew-it trap (Clue 2)
part1.script: Some pier kids wrote sticky notes about my marble test. Look at the time on each note. Drag it before the test or after the test. Which notes can we really check? Then a wrong prediction comes in. Is it useless?

part2.label: Part 2 · the flag lane (Clue 3)
part2.script: Drag the yellow flag to where you think the block will stop. Then roll the marble. The tape shows your gap. Do three trials on the low ramp, then change one thing: the ramp. Watch your gap meter.

explore.label: Part 3 · the Newton’s cradle (Clue 4)
explore.script: Here’s the Newton’s cradle. Pick how many balls to pull back. Predict how many will fly out. Then drag the end ball back and let go. Run three trials of each. Does the same thing happen every time?

assignment.label: Assignment · crack the case
assignment.script: Got all four clues? Crack the case at the top of this tab, and the envelopes open. Then make the speed limit sign. After that, answer two questions, fill in your trial table, and finish your C-E-R.

evidence.label: Use your evidence · CER
evidence.script: A classmate says one trial is enough. Is that true? Think about the bumpy trial on the flag lane, and the cradle. Pick your side, tap two pieces of evidence, then explain how they prove your claim.

closing.label: Case closed
closing.script: Case closed! The trials showed it: faster carts push farther, so the pier got a real speed limit. Your opened envelope goes in your Field Notebook. Next time: energy that changes from one form to another.

hlCoach.title: Highlight like a scientist
tips: Highlight key words, not whole paragraphs.
If everything is yellow, nothing stands out. Aim for a few words in each paragraph.
Look for words that are explained.
Bold words, and words followed by “means”, “is called” or a meaning in ( ), are often worth saving.
Look for answers to the Big Question.
Ask yourself: does this help me explain how trials and predictions find a pattern?
“Because”, “so” and “first … then” show how ideas connect.
Yellow = important. Green = evidence I might use in my answer. Pink = something I wonder about.

practice.q: Practice: tap the 3 to 5 words that matter most in this sentence.
practice.text: A prediction is written before the test, and many trials show a pattern you can trust.
practice.model: A scientist might highlight “prediction”, “before the test”, “many trials” and “pattern”. Those words hold the big idea. Small words like “a” and “the” don’t carry the idea.

hlCoach.outside: This works in every subject. When you read anything, save the words that answer your question, and skip the rest.
